# Appendix

## Derivation of EM 

The idea of EM is that, if we had the complete data, maximizing the complete likelihood would be simpler to account for the missing data. For the skewed tensor variate distributions, the missing values are the positive mixing variables $W_1,\dots,W_N$. The model is

$$
\tensor{X}_{i} = \tensor{M} + W_{i} \tensor{A} + \sqrt{W_{i}}\tensor{V}_{i},
\qquad
\tensor{V}_{i} \sim \mathcal{N}_{n^*}
\left(\mathbb{O}, \bigotimes_{d=1}^{D}\Sigma_{d}\right),
$$

where

$$
n^*=\prod_{d=1}^{D} n_d.
$$

If we knew the latent draws $W_{i} = w_{i}$, then the distribution of $X_{i}$ is tensor variate normal. 

$$\tensor{X}_{i}$$

Conditional on $W_i=w_i$, the vectorized tensor is multivariate normal:

$$
\ve{x}_i \mid w_i
\sim
N_{n^*}
\left(
\ve{m}+w_i\ve{a},
w_i\mat{K}_{\Sigma}
\right).
$$

The important point is that $w_i$ scales the full vectorized covariance matrix once. It is not the same as multiplying every mode covariance matrix by $w_i$, because

$$
\bigotimes_{d=1}^{D}(w_i\Sigma_d)
=
w_i^D
\bigotimes_{d=1}^{D}\Sigma_d.
$$

The intended covariance is instead

$$
w_i
\bigotimes_{d=1}^{D}\Sigma_d.
$$

Equivalently, the same full covariance could be represented by putting $w_i$ into one mode covariance,

$$
(w_i\Sigma_1)\otimes \Sigma_2 \otimes \cdots \otimes \Sigma_D
=
w_i
\bigotimes_{d=1}^{D}\Sigma_d,
$$

or by distributing $w_i^{1/D}$ across all modes,

$$
\bigotimes_{d=1}^{D}(w_i^{1/D}\Sigma_d)
=
w_i
\bigotimes_{d=1}^{D}\Sigma_d.
$$

The following matrix properties are used to derive the conditional density.

1. If $\mat{B}$ is a $p \times p$ matrix and $c>0$ is a scalar, then

$$
|c\mat{B}|=c^p|\mat{B}|.
$$

This holds because multiplying a $p \times p$ matrix by $c$ multiplies each of its $p$ rows by $c$.

2. If $\mat{B}$ is $p \times p$ and $\mat{C}$ is $q \times q$, then

$$
|\mat{B}\otimes\mat{C}|
=
|\mat{B}|^q|\mat{C}|^p.
$$

One way to see this is through eigenvalues. The eigenvalues of $\mat{B}\otimes\mat{C}$ are all products $\lambda_r(\mat{B})\lambda_s(\mat{C})$, so their product is $|\mat{B}|^q|\mat{C}|^p$.

Applying this property repeatedly gives

$$
\left|
\bigotimes_{d=1}^{D}\Sigma_d
\right|
=
\prod_{d=1}^{D}
|\Sigma_d|^{n^*/n_d}.
$$

3. The inverse of a scalar multiple and the inverse of a Kronecker product are

$$
(w_i\mat{K}_{\Sigma})^{-1}
=
\frac{1}{w_i}\mat{K}_{\Sigma}^{-1},
\qquad
\left(\bigotimes_{d=1}^{D}\Sigma_d\right)^{-1}
=
\bigotimes_{d=1}^{D}\Sigma_d^{-1}.
$$

The second identity follows from the mixed-product property

$$
(\mat{B}\otimes\mat{C})(\mat{D}\otimes\mat{E})
=
(\mat{B}\mat{D})\otimes(\mat{C}\mat{E}).
$$

Using the multivariate normal density with covariance $w_i\mat{K}_{\Sigma}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(\tensor{X}_i \mid w_i)
=&
(2\pi)^{-n^*/2}
\left|w_i\mat{K}_{\Sigma}\right|^{-1/2} \\
&\times
\exp\left\{
-\frac{1}{2}
\left(\ve{x}_i-\ve{m}-w_i\ve{a}\right)^T
\left(w_i\mat{K}_{\Sigma}\right)^{-1}
\left(\ve{x}_i-\ve{m}-w_i\ve{a}\right)
\right\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Now apply the determinant properties:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left|w_i\mat{K}_{\Sigma}\right|^{-1/2}
&=
\left(w_i^{n^*}|\mat{K}_{\Sigma}|\right)^{-1/2} \\
&=
w_i^{-n^*/2}
\left|\mat{K}_{\Sigma}\right|^{-1/2} \\
&=
w_i^{-n^*/2}
\prod_{d=1}^{D}
|\Sigma_d|^{-n^*/(2n_d)}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Also,

$$
\left(w_i\mat{K}_{\Sigma}\right)^{-1}
=
\frac{1}{w_i}\mat{P}_{\Sigma}.
$$

Therefore the correct conditional density is

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(\tensor{X}_i \mid w_i)
=&
(2\pi)^{-n^*/2}
w_i^{-n^*/2}
\left(
\prod_{d=1}^{D}
|\Sigma_d|^{-n^*/(2n_d)}
\right) \\
&\times
\exp\left\{
-\frac{1}{2w_i}
\operatorname{vec}(\tensor{X}_i-\tensor{M}-w_i\tensor{A})^T
\left(\bigotimes_{d=1}^{D}\Sigma_d^{-1}\right)
\operatorname{vec}(\tensor{X}_i-\tensor{M}-w_i\tensor{A})
\right\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

For the complete data, the joint density factors as

$$
f(\tensor{X}_i,w_i)
=
f(\tensor{X}_i\mid w_i)f_W(w_i).
$$

Let

$$
\ve{r}_i=\ve{x}_i-\ve{m},
\qquad
\delta_i=\ve{r}_i^T\mat{P}_{\Sigma}\ve{r}_i,
\qquad
\rho=\ve{a}^T\mat{P}_{\Sigma}\ve{a},
\qquad
\xi_i=\ve{r}_i^T\mat{P}_{\Sigma}\ve{a}.
$$

The quadratic term expands as

$$
\begin{aligned}
-\frac{1}{2w_i}
(\ve{r}_i-w_i\ve{a})^T
\mat{P}_{\Sigma}
(\ve{r}_i-w_i\ve{a})
&=
-\frac{1}{2w_i}
\left(
\delta_i
-2w_i\xi_i
+w_i^2\rho
\right) \\
&=
-\frac{1}{2w_i}\delta_i
+\xi_i
-\frac{w_i}{2}\rho.
\end{aligned}
$$

This is where the middle cross term loses its visible $w_i$: the $w_i$ from the shifted mean cancels with the $1/w_i$ from the conditional precision.

Summing over $N$ observations, the complete log-likelihood can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ell_C(\theta;\tensor{X},\ve{w})
=&
C
-
\sum_{d=1}^{D}
\frac{Nn^*}{2n_d}\log|\Sigma_d|
+ h(\ve{w}\mid \theta_W) \\
&+
\sum_{i=1}^{N}\xi_i
-
\frac{1}{2}
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
\frac{1}{w_i}\delta_i
-
\frac{1}{2}
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
w_i\rho,
\end{aligned}
$$

where the terms involving only the latent mixing distribution and the normalizing factor in $w_i$ are collected into

$$
h(\ve{w}\mid \theta_W)
=
\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log f_W(w_i;\theta_W)
-
\frac{n^*}{2}
\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log w_i.
$$

This explains why the determinant contribution from $w_i$ is not shown beside the $\log|\Sigma_d|$ terms in the compact complete log-likelihood: it is part of $h(\ve{w}\mid\theta_W)$.

### E-step

At iteration $t$, the E-step takes conditional expectations with respect to

$$
W_i \mid \tensor{X}_i,\theta^{(t)}.
$$

The three expectations needed in the common M-step are

$$
\eta_i
=
E(W_i\mid\tensor{X}_i,\theta^{(t)}),
\qquad
\tau_i
=
E(W_i^{-1}\mid\tensor{X}_i,\theta^{(t)}),
\qquad
\zeta_i
=
E(\log W_i\mid\tensor{X}_i,\theta^{(t)}).
$$

Using the complete log-likelihood, the conditional density of $W_i$ is proportional to

$$
f(w_i\mid \tensor{X}_i,\theta^{(t)})
\propto
w_i^{-n^*/2}
\exp\left\{
-\frac{\delta_i}{2w_i}
-\frac{\rho w_i}{2}
\right\}
f_W(w_i;\theta_W^{(t)}).
$$

The term $\exp(\xi_i)$ does not appear in this kernel because it does not depend on $w_i$.

For the four skewed models implemented here, this posterior kernel is a generalized inverse Gaussian distribution. We use the parameterization

$$
W \sim \operatorname{GIG}(\lambda,\chi,\psi)
$$

with density proportional to

$$
w^{\lambda-1}
\exp\left\{
-\frac{1}{2}
\left(
\frac{\chi}{w}
+\psi w
\right)
\right\},
\qquad
w>0.
$$

Under this parameterization,

$$
E(W^q)
=
\left(\frac{\chi}{\psi}\right)^{q/2}
\frac{
K_{\lambda+q}(\sqrt{\chi\psi})
}{
K_{\lambda}(\sqrt{\chi\psi})
},
$$

where $K_{\lambda}$ is the modified Bessel function of the third kind. This identity follows by multiplying the GIG density by $w^q$; the resulting integral has the same normalizing form with $\lambda$ replaced by $\lambda+q$.

Setting $q=1$ gives

$$
\eta_i
=
E(W_i\mid\tensor{X}_i)
=
\sqrt{\frac{\chi_i}{\psi_i}}
\frac{
K_{\lambda_i+1}(\sqrt{\chi_i\psi_i})
}{
K_{\lambda_i}(\sqrt{\chi_i\psi_i})
}.
$$

Setting $q=-1$ and using the Bessel recurrence relation gives

$$
\tau_i
=
E(W_i^{-1}\mid\tensor{X}_i)
=
\sqrt{\frac{\psi_i}{\chi_i}}
\frac{
K_{\lambda_i+1}(\sqrt{\chi_i\psi_i})
}{
K_{\lambda_i}(\sqrt{\chi_i\psi_i})
}
-
\frac{2\lambda_i}{\chi_i}.
$$

Differentiating $E(W^q)$ at $q=0$ gives

$$
\zeta_i
=
E(\log W_i\mid\tensor{X}_i)
=
\frac{1}{2}\log\left(\frac{\chi_i}{\psi_i}\right)
+
\frac{\partial}{\partial \lambda_i}
\log K_{\lambda_i}(\sqrt{\chi_i\psi_i}).
$$

The posterior GIG parameters are obtained by combining the conditional normal kernel above with the prior density of $W_i$:

$$
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
\text{Model} & \lambda_i & \chi_i & \psi_i \\
\hline
\text{Skewed-t} &
-(\nu+n^*)/2 &
\delta_i+\nu &
\rho \\
\text{Variance gamma} &
\gamma-n^*/2 &
\delta_i &
\rho+2\gamma \\
\text{Normal inverse Gaussian} &
-(n^*+1)/2 &
\delta_i+1 &
\rho+\kappa^2 \\
\text{Generalized hyperbolic} &
\lambda-n^*/2 &
\delta_i+\omega &
\rho+\omega
\end{array}
$$

### M-step

In the M-step, replace $w_i$, $w_i^{-1}$, and $\log w_i$ in the complete log-likelihood by $\eta_i$, $\tau_i$, and $\zeta_i$. The common part of the expected complete log-likelihood is

$$
\begin{aligned}
Q(\theta\mid\theta^{(t)})
=&
C
-
\sum_{d=1}^{D}
\frac{Nn^*}{2n_d}\log|\Sigma_d| \\
&+
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
\ve{r}_i^T\mat{P}_{\Sigma}\ve{a}
-
\frac{1}{2}
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
\tau_i
\ve{r}_i^T\mat{P}_{\Sigma}\ve{r}_i
-
\frac{1}{2}
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
\eta_i
\ve{a}^T\mat{P}_{\Sigma}\ve{a}
+
Q_W,
\end{aligned}
$$

where $Q_W$ contains the terms from $E\{\log f_W(W_i;\theta_W)\mid\tensor{X}_i\}$.

First hold the covariance matrices fixed and differentiate with respect to $\ve{m}$ and $\ve{a}$. The two first-order equations are

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
\tau_i(\ve{x}_i-\ve{m})
-
N\ve{a}
=
\ve{0},
$$

and

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
(\ve{x}_i-\ve{m})
-
\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N}\eta_i\right)\ve{a}
=
\ve{0}.
$$

Let

$$
\bar{\eta}
=
\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\eta_i,
\qquad
\bar{\tau}
=
\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\tau_i.
$$

Solving the two linear equations gives the updates

$$
\hat{\tensor{M}}
=
\frac{
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
(\bar{\eta}\tau_i-1)\tensor{X}_i
}{
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
(\bar{\eta}\tau_i-1)
},
$$

and

$$
\hat{\tensor{A}}
=
\frac{
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
(\bar{\tau}-\tau_i)\tensor{X}_i
}{
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
(\bar{\tau}\eta_i-1)
}.
$$

The covariance updates are a weighted version of the tensor normal flip-flop update. Let

$$
\tensor{R}_i
=
\tensor{X}_i-\hat{\tensor{M}},
$$

and let $\Sigma_{-j}$ denote the Kronecker product of all covariance matrices except $\Sigma_j$, ordered to match the mode-$j$ matricization. Define

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mat{S}_j
=
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
\bigg[
&\tau_i
\tensor{R}_{i(j)}
\Sigma_{-j}^{-1}
\tensor{R}_{i(j)}^T \\
&-
\tensor{R}_{i(j)}
\Sigma_{-j}^{-1}
\hat{\tensor{A}}_{(j)}^T
-
\hat{\tensor{A}}_{(j)}
\Sigma_{-j}^{-1}
\tensor{R}_{i(j)}^T \\
&+
\eta_i
\hat{\tensor{A}}_{(j)}
\Sigma_{-j}^{-1}
\hat{\tensor{A}}_{(j)}^T
\bigg].
\end{aligned}
$$

The part of $Q$ involving $\Sigma_j$ can be written as

$$
Q(\Sigma_j)
=
-
\frac{Nn^*}{2n_j}\log|\Sigma_j|
-
\frac{1}{2}
\operatorname{tr}
\left(
\Sigma_j^{-1}\mat{S}_j
\right).
$$

Using the differential identities

$$
d\log|\Sigma_j|
=
\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_j^{-1}d\Sigma_j),
$$

and

$$
d\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_j^{-1}\mat{S}_j)
=
-
\operatorname{tr}
\left(
\Sigma_j^{-1}
d\Sigma_j
\Sigma_j^{-1}
\mat{S}_j
\right),
$$

we get

$$
dQ(\Sigma_j)
=
\frac{1}{2}
\operatorname{tr}
\left[
\left(
-
\frac{Nn^*}{n_j}\Sigma_j^{-1}
+
\Sigma_j^{-1}\mat{S}_j\Sigma_j^{-1}
\right)
d\Sigma_j
\right].
$$

Setting this equal to zero for every $d\Sigma_j$ gives

$$
-\frac{Nn^*}{n_j}\Sigma_j^{-1} + \Sigma_j^{-1}\mat{S}_j\Sigma_j^{-1} = \mat{0}.
$$

Multiplying on the left and right by $\Sigma_j$ gives

$$
\hat{\Sigma}_j = \frac{n_j}{Nn^*} \mat{S}_j.
$$

Since the individual Kronecker factors are identifiable only up to compensating scale changes, the algorithm rescales the covariance matrices after each update. In \pkg{tensortools}, the traces of the first $D-1$ covariance matrices are normalized to their mode dimensions, and the final covariance matrix absorbs the product of the removed scales so that the full Kronecker covariance is preserved.


## Proof of Flip-Flop for TVN

Let $\tensor{X}_{1}, \dots, \tensor{X}_{K}$ be IID from

$$
TVN_{n_{1}, n_{2}, n_{3}}
(\tensor{M}, \mat{U}_{1}, \mat{U}_{2}, \mat{U}_{3}),
$$

or equivalently,

$$
\text{vec}(\tensor{X}_{k}) \sim
N\left(
\text{vec}(\tensor{M}),
\mat{U}_{3} \otimes \mat{U}_{2} \otimes \mat{U}_{1}
\right).
$$

Let $\tensor{Y}_{k} = \tensor{X}_{k} - \tensor{M}$, let $n_{-j} = \prod_{\ell \neq j} n_{\ell}$, and define

$$
\mat{U}_{-1} = \mat{U}_{3} \otimes \mat{U}_{2}, \qquad
\mat{U}_{-2} = \mat{U}_{3} \otimes \mat{U}_{1}, \qquad
\mat{U}_{-3} = \mat{U}_{2} \otimes \mat{U}_{1}.
$$

Up to a constant that does not depend on the parameters, the log-likelihood can be written using the mode-1 unfolding as

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ell
=& -\frac{K}{2}
\left[
 n_{2}n_{3}\log|\mat{U}_{1}|
+ n_{1}n_{3}\log|\mat{U}_{2}|
+ n_{1}n_{2}\log|\mat{U}_{3}|
\right] \\
& -\frac{1}{2}
\sum_{k=1}^{K}
\text{tr}\left[
\mat{U}_{1}^{-1}
\tensor{Y}_{k(1)}
(\mat{U}_{3} \otimes \mat{U}_{2})^{-1}
\tensor{Y}_{k(1)}^{T}
\right].
\end{aligned}
$$

More generally, using mode-$j$ matricization, the quadratic term is

$$
\text{tr}\left[
\mat{U}_{j}^{-1}
\tensor{Y}_{k(j)}
\mat{U}_{-j}^{-1}
\tensor{Y}_{k(j)}^{T}
\right],
$$

which is equivalent to the tensor inner-product notation

$$
\left\langle
\tensor{Y}_{k},
\tensor{Y}_{k}
\nProd{1}\mat{U}_{1}^{-1}
\nProd{2}\mat{U}_{2}^{-1}
\nProd{3}\mat{U}_{3}^{-1}
\right\rangle.
$$

In vectorized form, let

$$
\mat{\Omega} =
\mat{U}_{3} \otimes \mat{U}_{2} \otimes \mat{U}_{1}.
$$

The part of the log-likelihood involving $\tensor{M}$ is

$$
-\frac{1}{2}
\sum_{k=1}^{K}
\left[
\text{vec}(\tensor{X}_{k}) - \text{vec}(\tensor{M})
\right]^{T}
\mat{\Omega}^{-1}
\left[
\text{vec}(\tensor{X}_{k}) - \text{vec}(\tensor{M})
\right].
$$

Differentiating with respect to $\text{vec}(\tensor{M})$ gives

$$
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \text{vec}(\tensor{M})}
=
\mat{\Omega}^{-1}
\sum_{k=1}^{K}
\left[
\text{vec}(\tensor{X}_{k}) - \text{vec}(\tensor{M})
\right].
$$

Setting this equal to zero gives

$$
\hat{\tensor{M}} =
\bar{\tensor{X}} =
\frac{1}{K}
\sum_{k=1}^{K}\tensor{X}_{k}.
$$

Now hold the other covariance matrices fixed and estimate $\mat{U}_{j}$. Define

$$
\mat{S}_{j}
=
\sum_{k=1}^{K}
\tensor{Y}_{k(j)}
\mat{U}_{-j}^{-1}
\tensor{Y}_{k(j)}^{T}.
$$

The part of the log-likelihood involving $\mat{U}_{j}$ is

$$
\ell_{j}
=
-\frac{K n_{-j}}{2}\log|\mat{U}_{j}|
-\frac{1}{2}
\text{tr}\left(
\mat{U}_{j}^{-1}\mat{S}_{j}
\right).
$$

Using

$$
d\log|\mat{U}_{j}| =
\text{tr}(\mat{U}_{j}^{-1}d\mat{U}_{j})
$$

and

$$
d\text{tr}(\mat{U}_{j}^{-1}\mat{S}_{j})
=
-\text{tr}
\left(
\mat{U}_{j}^{-1}
d\mat{U}_{j}
\mat{U}_{j}^{-1}
\mat{S}_{j}
\right),
$$

the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}
d\ell_{j}
=& -\frac{K n_{-j}}{2}
\text{tr}(\mat{U}_{j}^{-1}d\mat{U}_{j}) \\
&+ \frac{1}{2}
\text{tr}
\left(
\mat{U}_{j}^{-1}
d\mat{U}_{j}
\mat{U}_{j}^{-1}
\mat{S}_{j}
\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

Moving $d\mat{U}_{j}$ to the end of each trace gives

$$
d\ell_{j}
=
\frac{1}{2}
\text{tr}
\left[
\left(
-K n_{-j}\mat{U}_{j}^{-1}
+ \mat{U}_{j}^{-1}\mat{S}_{j}\mat{U}_{j}^{-1}
\right)
d\mat{U}_{j}
\right].
$$

Since this must be zero for all $d\mat{U}_{j}$,

$$
-K n_{-j}\mat{U}_{j}^{-1}
+ \mat{U}_{j}^{-1}\mat{S}_{j}\mat{U}_{j}^{-1}
=
\mat{0}.
$$

Multiplying on the left and right by $\mat{U}_{j}$ gives

$$
\hat{\mat{U}}_{j}
=
\frac{1}{K n_{-j}}
\mat{S}_{j}.
$$

Substituting back the definition of $\mat{S}_{j}$ gives the three TVN updates:

$$
\hat{\mat{U}}_{1}
=
\frac{1}{K n_{2}n_{3}}
\sum_{k=1}^{K}
(\tensor{X}_{k}-\bar{\tensor{X}})_{(1)}
(\hat{\mat{U}}_{3}\otimes\hat{\mat{U}}_{2})^{-1}
(\tensor{X}_{k}-\bar{\tensor{X}})_{(1)}^{T},
$$

$$
\hat{\mat{U}}_{2}
=
\frac{1}{K n_{1}n_{3}}
\sum_{k=1}^{K}
(\tensor{X}_{k}-\bar{\tensor{X}})_{(2)}
(\hat{\mat{U}}_{3}\otimes\hat{\mat{U}}_{1})^{-1}
(\tensor{X}_{k}-\bar{\tensor{X}})_{(2)}^{T},
$$

and

$$
\hat{\mat{U}}_{3}
=
\frac{1}{K n_{1}n_{2}}
\sum_{k=1}^{K}
(\tensor{X}_{k}-\bar{\tensor{X}})_{(3)}
(\hat{\mat{U}}_{2}\otimes\hat{\mat{U}}_{1})^{-1}
(\tensor{X}_{k}-\bar{\tensor{X}})_{(3)}^{T}.
$$

Because each covariance update depends on the other two covariance estimates, the MLEs are found by iterating these equations. The individual $\mat{U}_{j}$ are determined only up to scale constraints; the Kronecker product is the identifiable covariance structure.
